title: Before sunrise and sunset
hook: be patient and glorify before sunrise and before sunset (20:130)

segments.voice: Yesterday: 'ilm, knowledge increased, and your line was rabbi zidni 'ilma. What was the one new thing you learned? Day four hundred seventy-nine, our last day in Ta-Ha.

A day has two edges. The first few minutes after you wake, before the world gets in. And the last stretch of light in the afternoon, when the shadows go long and the day starts to close. In between them sits everything else the day brings. Ta-Ha, near its end, tells the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who is hearing hard words from his opponents, what to do at both edges. It starts with patience.

Verse one hundred thirty, in Pickthall's words: bear with what they say, "and celebrate the praises of thy Lord ere the rising of the sun and ere the going down thereof." The verb is sabbih: glorify, say subhan Allah, God is far above every fault. It's tasbih, the same root as the opening of Al-Isra, glory to Him who carried His servant by night. Then the verse adds more times: some hours of the night, and the ends of the day. Like the dawn verse in Al-Isra a couple of weeks back, commentators read this one as a map of the prayer times. Before sunrise is Fajr. Before sunset is 'Asr, the afternoon prayer. The hours of the night hold Maghrib and 'Isha. A hadith in Sahih Muslim singles out the two edges: the Prophet said that whoever prays before the rising of the sun and before its setting will not enter the Fire. And the verse ends with a reason, la'allaka tarda: so that you may be content, well pleased. That's the surprising part. The command doesn't end in duty or reward, but in contentment. The man being mocked is told: glorify at both ends of the day, and you'll find peace. Beyond the prayers, some Muslims keep morning and evening remembrances, the adhkar, short phrases said as the day opens and as it closes. One of the simplest, from a hadith in Bukhari: subhan Allah wa bi-hamdihi, glory to God and praise to Him. Ta-Ha opened by saying the Qur'an wasn't sent to wear anyone out. It closes by giving the day a frame of praise at both edges, so that the middle, with all its hard words, can be borne.
screen: `BEAR WITH WHAT THEY SAY.` · `SABBIH: SAY GOD IS FAR ABOVE FAULT.` · `FAJR AND 'ASR AT THE EDGES.` · `LA'ALLAKA TARDA: THAT YOU BE CONTENT.` · then, large: `GLORY AT BOTH EDGES.`

segments.voice: The practice is a tasbih at both edges of the day. Wherever you are in your day now, sit, and say it once, slowly, aloud or under your breath: subhan Allah. If you're not Muslim, you can sit with the plain meaning: glory beyond anything I can name. Then choose two moments: this evening's last light, before dinner, and tomorrow's first minutes after you wake. Decide where you'll be for each. Say it once more, quietly, to mark the plan. The bell holds the time.
Tasbih. Glorifying God at the two edges of the day, with patience in between, so that you may be content. Today's word.
Your line: glory at both edges. This evening before sunset, and tomorrow before sunrise, say one tasbih and notice the edge of the day. Day four hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims pray Fajr before sunrise and 'Asr before sunset among the five daily prayers, and some recite the morning and evening adhkar, including subhan Allah wa bi-hamdihi, at the two ends of the day.

fork.setup: people are saying hurtful things about you every day. what does 20:130 tell the Prophet to do first?
options: bear with what they say, and glorify God before sunrise and before sunset.
fork.reveal: patience, then praise at both edges of the day, so that you may be content.

original.note: Arabic: glory be to God, the tasbih, from the root of sabbih in 20:130.

trapdoor: what you thought: pray in the morning and evening.
what it means: in the face of hard words, glorify God at the day's two edges and through the night, and contentment follows.
what a scholar hears: tafsir maps 20:130 onto the five prayers; Muslim's hadith on praying before sunrise and sunset singles out Fajr and 'Asr.
